notes.definition: A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise by differentiation.
explanation: Most cells in an adult animal are differentiated: they have become specialised to do one job, such as a nerve cell or a muscle cell, and they cannot change into a different type. Stem cells are different. They are undifferentiated, so they have not yet specialised. They can divide by mitosis to produce many more stem cells, and they can differentiate to become other, specialised types of cell. Animals and plants both have stem cells, but they are found in different places and can produce different ranges of cells.

Stem cells in embryos can differentiate into most types of cell in the body, which is how a single fertilised egg develops into a whole organism. Stem cells taken from human embryos can be cloned (grown to produce many identical cells) and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells. In adult animals stem cells are mainly used to repair and replace cells. Adult stem cells are more limited: for example, stem cells in adult bone marrow can form many types of cells, including blood cells, but not every type of cell.

In plants, stem cells are found in meristem tissue at the tips of roots and shoots. Meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the whole life of the plant. This is why plants can keep growing new roots, leaves and flowers. Meristem cells can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. Rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction, and crop plants with special features, such as disease resistance, can be cloned to produce large numbers of identical plants for farmers.

Treatment with stem cells may be able to help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis. For example, stem cells might be made to differentiate into insulin-producing cells for people with type 1 diabetes, or into nerve cells for people whose spinal cord has been damaged. In therapeutic cloning an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from this embryo are not rejected by the patient's body because they are genetically identical to the patient's own cells, so they may be used for medical treatment.

The use of stem cells has potential risks and raises ethical issues. Stem cells grown in the laboratory could become contaminated with a virus, so there is a risk of transferring a viral infection to the patient. Some people have ethical or religious objections to using embryos, because the embryo is destroyed when the stem cells are removed and they believe an embryo has a right to life. Others argue that the embryos used are often spare ones from fertility treatment that would be destroyed anyway, and that the potential to cure serious diseases outweighs these concerns. You should be able to evaluate these practical risks and benefits and the social and ethical issues.
keyFacts: A stem cell is undifferentiated and can divide to make more stem cells and differentiate into other cell types.
Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into most types of human cell.
Adult bone marrow stem cells can form many types of cell, including blood cells.
Plant meristems (root and shoot tips) can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life.
Stem cell treatments may help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.
Therapeutic cloning produces an embryo with the same genes as the patient, so the stem cells are not rejected.
Risks include transfer of viral infection; some people have ethical or religious objections to using embryos.
Meristem cloning produces plant clones quickly and cheaply, for example to save rare species or produce disease-resistant crops.
Knowledge of stem cell techniques is not required by AQA.

keyTerms.definition: An undifferentiated cell that can give rise to many more cells of the same type and from which certain other cells can arise by differentiation.
Not yet specialised for a particular function.
The process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function.
A stem cell from an early embryo that can differentiate into most types of human cell.
A stem cell found in adult tissues, such as bone marrow, that can form a limited range of cell types, including blood cells.
Plant tissue at the tips of roots and shoots containing stem cells that can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life.
Producing an embryo with the same genes as a patient, so that its stem cells can be used for treatment without being rejected.
When the patient's immune system attacks transplanted cells or tissue because it recognises them as foreign.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why therapeutic cloning avoids rejection
workedExamples.question: Explain why stem cells produced by therapeutic cloning are not rejected by the patient.
steps: Identify the key idea: the embryo in therapeutic cloning is made with the same genes as the patient.
So the stem cells taken from it are genetically identical to the patient's own cells.
The patient's immune system does not recognise them as foreign, so it does not attack them.
workedExamples.answer: The embryo has the same genes as the patient, so the stem cells are genetically identical to the patient's cells and are not recognised as foreign by the immune system.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a source of stem cells
workedExamples.question: A doctor wants to treat a patient whose spinal cord has been damaged, causing paralysis. Suggest why embryonic stem cells might be more useful than stem cells from the patient's bone marrow.
steps: The treatment needs new nerve cells.
Adult bone marrow stem cells can only form a limited range of cell types, mainly blood cells.
Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into most types of human cell, including nerve cells.
workedExamples.answer: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into most cell types, including nerve cells, whereas bone marrow stem cells mainly form blood cells.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a use of stem cells
workedExamples.question: Give one benefit and one risk of using stem cells to treat type 1 diabetes.
steps: Benefit: think about what the treatment could achieve. Stem cells could be made to differentiate into cells that produce insulin.
This could mean the patient no longer needs insulin injections.
Risk: think about the cells being grown in a laboratory. They could be contaminated and transfer a viral infection.
workedExamples.answer: Benefit: could produce insulin-secreting cells so the patient no longer needs injections. Risk: transfer of a viral infection from contaminated stem cells.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think adult stem cells can become any type of cell.
misconceptions.right: In fact adult stem cells, such as those in bone marrow, can only form a limited range of cell types, including blood cells. Embryonic stem cells can form most types of human cell.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think therapeutic cloning produces a baby.
misconceptions.right: In fact the embryo is only used as a source of stem cells for treatment. It is not allowed to develop into a baby.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plant stem cells stop working once the plant is fully grown.
misconceptions.right: In fact meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the whole life of the plant.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think stem cell treatments are risk-free because the cells are human.
misconceptions.right: In fact there are risks, such as transferring a viral infection if the cultured stem cells are contaminated.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say stem cells from a donor embryo are never rejected.
misconceptions.right: In fact donor stem cells can be rejected. Only stem cells with the same genes as the patient, such as those from therapeutic cloning, avoid rejection.

realWorld: Bone marrow transplants use stem cells from a donor's bone marrow to treat leukaemia: the stem cells produce new healthy blood cells in the patient.
Scientists are researching ways to make stem cells differentiate into insulin-producing cells to treat type 1 diabetes, and into nerve cells to treat paralysis.
Seed banks and botanic gardens use meristem cloning (tissue culture) to produce many copies of rare and endangered plants such as some orchids.
Commercial growers clone disease-resistant banana and potato plants from meristems so that farmers get large numbers of identical, healthy plants.
examTips: Learn the definition of a stem cell word for word: an undifferentiated cell which can give rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise by differentiation.
For 'evaluate' questions, give benefits AND risks or objections, then finish with a justified conclusion. One-sided answers cannot reach the top level.
When explaining why therapeutic cloning avoids rejection, say the embryo (and therefore the stem cells) has the same genes as the patient. 'Same DNA' is also acceptable; 'same cells' is not.
Do not write about lab techniques for growing stem cells: they are not required and gain no marks.
Compare sources precisely: embryonic = most types of human cell; adult bone marrow = many types including blood cells; meristem = any type of plant cell, throughout life.
summary: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and differentiate into other cell types.
Embryonic stem cells can become most types of human cell; adult bone marrow stem cells form many types, including blood cells.
Plant meristems can form any type of plant cell throughout the life of the plant.
Stem cells may help treat diabetes and paralysis.
Therapeutic cloning makes an embryo with the patient's genes, so the stem cells are not rejected.
Risks include viral infection; some people have ethical or religious objections to using embryos.
Meristem cloning produces identical plants quickly and cheaply, to save rare species and grow useful crops.

questions.question: Which statement describes a stem cell?
options: A cell that has become specialised
A cell with no nucleus
An undifferentiated cell that can become other types of cell
A cell found only in plants
markScheme: 1 mark: an undifferentiated cell that can become other types of cell
questions.explanation: Stem cells are undifferentiated and can differentiate into other cell types. Specialised cells have already differentiated, and stem cells are found in both animals and plants.

questions.question: Where are stem cells found in plants?
options: Meristems
Xylem
Guard cells
Palisade cells
markScheme: 1 mark: meristems
questions.explanation: Plant stem cells are in meristem tissue at root and shoot tips. Xylem, guard cells and palisade cells are specialised cells.

questions.question: Stem cells from adult bone marrow can form many types of cell. Which type of cell is an example?
options: Root hair cells
Red blood cells
Egg cells
Xylem cells
markScheme: 1 mark: red blood cells
questions.explanation: Bone marrow stem cells form blood cells such as red and white blood cells. Root hair and xylem cells are plant cells, and egg cells are gametes made in the ovaries.

questions.question: Which type of stem cell can differentiate into the widest range of human cells?
options: Adult bone marrow stem cells
Adult skin stem cells
Meristem cells
Embryonic stem cells
markScheme: 1 mark: embryonic stem cells
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells can become most types of human cell. Adult stem cells form a limited range, and meristem cells are plant cells.

questions.question: In therapeutic cloning, why are the stem cells not rejected by the patient?
options: The stem cells are too small to be detected
The patient takes antibiotics
The embryo has the same genes as the patient
The stem cells come from a close relative
markScheme: 1 mark: the embryo has the same genes as the patient
questions.explanation: Therapeutic cloning produces an embryo with the same genes as the patient, so the immune system does not see the cells as foreign. A relative's cells are not genetically identical and could still be rejected; antibiotics kill bacteria and do not prevent rejection.

questions.question: Which is a practical risk of using stem cells in medical treatment?
options: Transfer of a viral infection
The patient will become a clone
The stem cells cause diabetes
The patient's DNA changes to match the stem cells
markScheme: 1 mark: transfer of a viral infection
questions.explanation: Stem cells grown in a laboratory could be contaminated with viruses, which could be transferred to the patient. The other options are not real risks.

questions.question: A gardener takes a few cells from the shoot tip of a rare plant and grows them into hundreds of new plants. Which statement about the new plants is correct?
options: They show a wide range of genetic variation
They can only form leaf cells
They will all be infertile
They are genetically identical to the parent plant
markScheme: 1 mark: they are genetically identical to the parent plant
questions.explanation: Meristem cells divide by mitosis and differentiate into all plant cell types, producing clones that are genetically identical to the parent. This is why the method is useful for rare species but also means there is no genetic variation.

questions.question: Why can a mature oak tree still grow new branches but an adult human cannot grow a new arm?
options: Human cells cannot divide by mitosis
Meristem cells in the tree can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout its life, but adult human stem cells form only a limited range of cells
Trees do not have differentiated cells
Adult humans have no stem cells at all
markScheme: 1 mark: meristem cells can form any plant cell throughout life; adult human stem cells are limited
questions.explanation: Plant meristems keep the ability to form any plant cell for the plant's whole life. Adult humans do have stem cells and their cells do divide by mitosis, but adult stem cells can only form a limited range of cell types.

questions.question: Which condition might be treated in future using stem cells?
options: A broken bone caused by a fall
Paralysis
A bacterial throat infection
Short-sightedness
markScheme: 1 mark: paralysis
questions.explanation: Stem cells may be able to replace damaged nerve cells in paralysis. Bacterial infections are treated with antibiotics, and short-sightedness with lenses.

questions.question: A farmer wants a large number of crop plants that all have the same disease resistance. Which method is most suitable?
options: Collect seeds from many different wild plants
Use embryonic stem cells from animals
Clone plants from the meristem of one disease-resistant plant
Grow plants from bone marrow cells
markScheme: 1 mark: clone plants from the meristem of one disease-resistant plant
questions.explanation: Meristem cloning quickly produces many plants genetically identical to the disease-resistant parent. Seeds from different wild plants would vary genetically.

questions.question: State what is meant by an undifferentiated cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: a cell that is not (yet) specialised
questions.explanation: An undifferentiated cell has not yet become specialised for a particular function.

questions.question: Name one place in an adult human where stem cells are found.
markScheme: 1 mark: bone marrow
questions.explanation: Adult bone marrow contains stem cells that form many types of cell, including blood cells.

questions.question: Give two reasons why plants are cloned from meristem tissue.
acceptedAnswers: large numbers of identical crop plants
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: quick / cheap (economical) / protect rare species from extinction / produce large numbers of identical crop plants / plants with special features such as disease resistance
questions.explanation: Meristem cloning is quick and economical and produces identical plants, which helps conserve rare species and gives farmers many plants with useful features.

questions.question: Describe the function of stem cells in an embryo and in an adult animal.
acceptedAnswers: embryo: differentiate into all cell types
markScheme: 1 mark: embryo: differentiate into most / all the types of cell needed to form the organism
1 mark: adult: replace or repair damaged / worn-out cells
questions.explanation: In embryos stem cells build all the tissues of the body. In adults they mainly replace and repair cells, such as producing new blood cells.

questions.question: Give one reason why some people object to the use of embryonic stem cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: the embryo is destroyed when stem cells are removed
1 mark: some people believe an embryo has a right to life / is a potential human / religious beliefs
questions.explanation: Removing stem cells destroys the embryo. People who believe life begins at conception, often for religious reasons, see this as ending a life.

questions.question: Suggest how stem cells could be used to treat a person with type 1 diabetes, who cannot produce insulin.
markScheme: 1 mark: stem cells made to differentiate into cells that produce insulin (pancreas cells)
1 mark: these cells are transplanted into the patient so they can make their own insulin
questions.explanation: If stem cells can be made into insulin-secreting cells and transplanted, the patient's body could produce insulin itself, reducing the need for injections.

questions.question: Explain why stem cells from a donor embryo might be rejected by a patient, but stem cells from therapeutic cloning would not.
markScheme: 1 mark: donor stem cells have different genes so the immune system recognises them as foreign / attacks them
1 mark: therapeutic cloning produces an embryo with the same genes as the patient so the cells are not recognised as foreign
questions.explanation: Rejection happens when the immune system detects cells that are genetically different. Cells from therapeutic cloning match the patient's genes.

questions.question: A scientist suggests using a patient's own bone marrow stem cells to repair damaged heart muscle. Suggest one advantage and two possible problems of this idea.
acceptedAnswers: may not differentiate into heart muscle
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: not rejected as same genes / no embryo is destroyed so fewer ethical objections
1 mark: problem: adult stem cells form a limited range of cells so may not become heart muscle
1 mark: problem: risk of viral infection if the cells become contaminated / cells might divide uncontrollably
questions.explanation: Using the patient's own cells avoids rejection and ethical issues, but bone marrow stem cells mainly make blood cells, so they may not form heart muscle cells; lab-grown cells also carry an infection risk.

questions.question: A rare species of plant has only five individuals left in the wild. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using meristem cloning to increase its numbers.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: produces large numbers of plants quickly / protects the species from extinction
1 mark: disadvantage: all clones are genetically identical so there is no variation; a single disease could kill them all
questions.explanation: Cloning rescues numbers fast, but identical plants share the same weaknesses, so the population could be wiped out by one disease or environmental change.

questions.question: Some embryos used for stem cell research are spare embryos from fertility treatment. Suggest why some people think using these embryos is more acceptable than creating new embryos for research.
acceptedAnswers: not created only to be destroyed
markScheme: 1 mark: the spare embryos would be destroyed / discarded anyway
1 mark: so no extra embryos are created just to be destroyed / the research gives a benefit from something otherwise wasted
questions.explanation: The argument is that because these embryos will not be used and would be destroyed, using them for research that may cure disease does more good, without creating extra embryos.

questions.question: State what happens when a cell differentiates.
markScheme: 1 mark: it becomes specialised (for a particular function)
questions.explanation: Differentiation is the process by which a cell gains the features it needs for a particular job.

questions.question: Compare the stem cells found in plant meristems with the stem cells found in adult human bone marrow.
markScheme: 1 mark: meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell (throughout the plant's life)
1 mark: bone marrow stem cells form only a limited range of cell types, such as blood cells
questions.explanation: Meristems remain able to form every plant cell type for life, while adult bone marrow stem cells are restricted mainly to forming blood cells.

questions.question: Bone marrow transplants are used to treat some blood cancers. Explain why a transplant from a donor needs the donor to be a close tissue match to the patient.
markScheme: 1 mark: the patient's immune system may recognise donor cells as foreign
1 mark: a close match (similar genes) reduces the risk of rejection
questions.explanation: Donor cells are not genetically identical to the patient, so they risk rejection. Choosing a donor whose cells are very similar reduces this risk.

questions.question:
Scientists are researching the use of embryonic stem cells from therapeutic cloning to treat people with paralysis.
Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells from therapeutic cloning for this treatment.
markScheme: Indicative content. Benefits: embryonic stem cells can differentiate into most types of cell, including nerve cells; could repair spinal cord damage and restore movement; improves quality of life; therapeutic cloning gives an embryo with the same genes as the patient; so cells are not rejected; no need for immunosuppressant drugs; no waiting for a donor. Risks and issues: risk of transfer of viral infection from cultured cells; treatment may not work or the cells may not differentiate correctly; the embryo is destroyed; ethical or religious objections that the embryo has a right to life; expensive and still being researched; long-term effects unknown. Conclusion: a justified judgement, for example the benefits may outweigh the risks if safety is proven.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a balanced evaluation with benefits and risks or ethical issues, both explained, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some benefits and some risks or issues given, with some explanation, but conclusion missing or not justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple, one-sided statements of benefits or drawbacks.
questions.explanation: Evaluate means weigh up both sides and reach a judgement. Strong answers explain why the cells are useful (they can become nerve cells and are not rejected), give the risks (viral infection) and ethical objections (embryo destroyed), and finish with a reasoned conclusion.

questions.question: Describe the differences between stem cells from human embryos, stem cells from adult bone marrow and stem cells in plant meristems.
markScheme: Indicative content: embryonic stem cells can be cloned and made to differentiate into most types of human cell; their use involves destroying an embryo; adult bone marrow stem cells form many types of cell including blood cells but a more limited range; can be taken from the patient's own body; meristem cells are found at root and shoot tips; can differentiate into any type of plant cell; throughout the life of the plant; used to clone plants quickly and cheaply.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear differences given for all three sources, including the range of cells each can form.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of one or two sources with little comparison.
questions.explanation: The key difference is the range of cells each type can produce: embryonic (most human cells), adult bone marrow (limited, including blood cells), meristem (any plant cell for life).

questions.question: A plant nursery grows a rare orchid. Describe how meristem tissue allows the nursery to produce many orchids, and explain why this is useful.
markScheme: Indicative content: meristem tissue found at the shoot or root tips; contains stem cells (undifferentiated); cells divide by mitosis; can differentiate into any type of plant cell; so a small piece can grow into a whole new plant; clones are genetically identical to the parent; quick and economical; large numbers produced; protects a rare species from extinction; can sell plants without taking from the wild.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links the properties of meristem cells to producing whole plants, and explains at least one benefit.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'they clone the plant', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Because meristem cells can become any plant cell, a tiny sample can grow into a complete identical plant. This is quick and cheap and can save rare species from extinction.

questions.question: Name the type of cloning in which an embryo is produced with the same genes as a patient.
markScheme: 1 mark: therapeutic cloning
questions.explanation: Therapeutic cloning produces an embryo genetically matched to the patient so its stem cells can be used in treatment.

questions.question: A muscle cell taken from an adult cannot be used to grow nerve cells, but an embryonic stem cell can. What is the best explanation?
options: The muscle cell has fewer chromosomes
The muscle cell has no genes for nerve cells
The muscle cell is already differentiated, so it cannot become a different type of cell
Muscle cells cannot divide by mitosis at all
markScheme: 1 mark: the muscle cell is already differentiated
questions.explanation: Most animal cells lose the ability to differentiate into other types once they have specialised. The muscle cell has the same chromosomes and genes as other body cells; it is its specialised state that prevents it becoming a nerve cell.
